claims.text: A conventional W–Cu composite has distinct tungsten and copper phases separated by an interface with relatively high thermal resistance.
A nano-engineered graded copper interlayer at W–Cu boundaries will form a seamless heterointerface.
Depositing the graded copper interlayer will produce a continuous, well-bonded W–Cu interface.
The graded interlayer will minimize discontinuities between tungsten and copper.
The graded copper layer will create a continuous lattice transition between tungsten and copper.
A continuous W–Cu lattice transition will reduce interfacial thermal resistance.
Reduced interfacial thermal resistance will enhance phonon-mediated heat transfer in the W–Cu composite.
The robust engineered interface will maintain the mechanical integrity of the W–Cu composite.
The engineered interface will resist irradiation-induced defects.
A W–Cu composite containing the graded copper interlayer will have higher thermal conductivity than an otherwise comparable standard W–Cu composite.
The modified composite will retain comparable or improved mechanical durability under extreme operating conditions.
The modified composite will retain comparable or improved irradiation resistance under extreme operating conditions.
Standard W–Cu composites typically have higher interfacial thermal resistance than the proposed modified composites.
Standard W–Cu composites may suffer durability degradation under severe conditions.
Standard W–Cu composites may suffer irradiation-resistance degradation under severe conditions.
The predicted benefits depend on the copper interlayer remaining continuous and well-adhered under operational stresses.
Thermal cycling that compromises the interlayer can negate the proposed performance gains.
Cu-modified seamless heterointerface engineering has previously been demonstrated in graphitic films for highly conductive, structurally stable thermal-management materials.
Direct evidence that this strategy improves irradiation resistance in W–Cu composites is lacking.
